title: No two marbled papers match, so Benjamin Franklin put marbling on banknotes

cover.alt: Close-up of a marbling bath: white, blue and brown paint floats in feathery swirls around drops of green, with a hand at the top edge.

body: Marbling floats drops of colour on a bath of thickened water, called **size**, and then combs and styluses drag them into feathers, waves or flowers. A sheet of paper laid on the surface picks up the whole design, so every print is a **one-off**. That made marbled paper useful for security: in 1775 Benjamin Franklin obtained English marbled paper to print the Continental Congress’s $20 note, and the Bank of England issued partly marbled cheques until the 1810s.

slides.alt: A hand pulls a fine stylus through drops of green paint floating among white and blue swirls, dragging them into pointed leaf shapes.
slides.caption: Ebru, Turkish-style marbling: drops of green paint float on a bath of thickened water, and a stylus drags them into leaves. Paper laid on top would pick up the whole design.

slides.heading: Match each name for marbling
slides.explanation: Suminagashi is the oldest known form. Ebru, the modern Turkish word, is related to the Persian abrī, which Annemarie Schimmel translated as ‘clouded paper’.

slides.question: What is the thickened bath that the colours float on called?
slides.explanation: Size was traditionally made from plant gums such as gum tragacanth. Since the late 19th century, carrageenan from seaweed has been used.
